meta.sourceSheet: worksheet 'map-cards' of the designer spreadsheet (crate columns), plus the rulebook for the seat-scaling tables. The VP column of that sheet was SUPERSEDED by the flat island (2026-08-09) and its money column was superseded by v31 (02/09/2026), which deleted coins outright. Only the crate columns are still live source.
notes: THE FLAT ISLAND (Dean, 2026-08-09), unchanged by v31 and still the shape of the whole board. Every tile in play is mechanically identical: 2 crates of 2 cards, 6 VP to the first deliverer and 3 VP to the second. There is no level gate, no ascending 4/8/16 size gradient, no per-level fill-order bonus and no level-3 end trigger. The game ends when any one seat completes its 6th island delivery. Everything that used to be decided by a tile's LEVEL is decided by its DELIVERY ORDER, which is the single gradient left in the island and the only thing worth racing for.

LEVEL IS NOW ART. `tiles[].level` and `slotsBySeats` survive because the physical island is still built as a pyramid out of the printed map cards, and the bookend rule below still decides which faces are on the table. Nothing mechanical reads a level. If you find yourself adding a rule keyed to level, you are re-introducing the hierarchy that was deleted in 2026-08; price it as a new rule, not as a restoration.

THE MEEPLES ARE THE ISLAND'S SECOND REWARD (Dean, 02/09/2026, v31), and they replace the coin. Each of the two delivery spaces on every tile carries ONE meeple, drawn from the bag and placed FACE UP at setup, visible to everybody all game. Claiming a delivery space takes its meeple with the VP; the meeple goes to your personal supply and is spent at the start of a later turn to perform its colour's plain action, one at a time, after which it LEAVES THE GAME. So the island now pays in tempo rather than in currency, and it pays it VISIBLY: at setup the whole table can read which actions the board is offering and in what order, which is the first time in this design that the island has been legible before anybody delivers to it. The colour-to-action map is deliberately NOT duplicated here - a meeple performs the same plain action as that colour's Notice Board door, and workers.json is the one place that says what those are.

THE POOL IS 5 OF EACH OF THE 5 COLOURS, 25 IN A BAG, and colours are dealt from ALL FIVE suits regardless of which suits are at the table. A meeple of a suit nobody is farming still works, because the five actions exist regardless of who farms what, and dealing from the full five is what keeps the setup ritual identical at every seat count. ONE PROPERTY TO READ BEFORE TUNING THIS: 12 meeples are dealt at 2 seats, 18 at 3 and 24 at 4, against a bag of 25, so at 4 seats the island's colour mix is very nearly deterministic (24 of 25 drawn) while at 2 seats it is a genuine random sample of under half the bag. The variance in what the island offers is therefore highest at the seat count with the fewest players to compete for it. That is an accident of the numbers rather than a decision, and it is what overlays/meeple-pool-deep-v1.overlay.json exists to probe. poolSize is stored rather than derived so that an overlay moving perColour has to move it too, and data.test.ts asserts the two agree.

A MEEPLE NOBODY SPENDS IS A DEAD COMPONENT. The supply has no cap and no upkeep, and a meeple can only be spent at the start of a turn, so the failure mode to watch is a pile of them accumulating in front of a seat that never finds a turn to burn them. The simulator's new meeple-economy assertion counts earned against spent for exactly this reason; if unspent meeples climb through the game, the rule to reach for is the start-of-turn restriction, not the pool.

vpByDeliveryOrder is the whole VP schedule and the whole capacity rule at once: entry i is the VP taken by the (i+1)th delivery to a tile, and the array's LENGTH is how many deliveries a tile accepts. There is deliberately no separate deliveriesPerTile knob. Lengthening the array is the only way to open a third delivery space, which forces the question 'and what is it worth?' to be answered in the same edit - and since v31 it forces a second question too, because a third space would need a third meeple on the tile and the bag is only 25 deep. 6 then 3 is the time gradient in its entirety: being first to a tile is worth double being second, it is printed on the tile rather than on a chit strip beside the board, and it needs no per-player-count row in the teach. It replaced fillOrderBonusBySeats - see Rulebook/outstanding-rule-changes.md change 4 for why two overlapping decaying rewards was one too many.

tileRule replaces the old levelRules. crates x cardsPerCrate = 4 barn cards, at every tile, at every seat count. HISTORY, so nobody re-derives the old numbers off the sheet: ticket 14 read the printed quantity label as 2=/3=/3= and settled 2/6/9 on 2026-08-02; ticket 38 overturned it the same day to 2/4/6; the flat island overturned both on 2026-08-09. PRINT CONSEQUENCE: every tile face must show TWO crates and the label 2=, so the map-cards worksheet needs its crate count and quantity label reworked at levels 1 and 3.

coinsPerDelivery IS A TOMBSTONE, PINNED AT 0. v31 deleted coins from the game and the island pays a meeple instead, so this can never be anything but 0 - it is kept, at 0, only because the v31 plan named it explicitly rather than deleting the key, and because leaving it visible is a louder record than a silent removal for anybody arriving from a pre-v31 report. It has NO KNOB: there is no coin for a sweep to mint. If a later pass tidies the key away, nothing reads it.

cardsPerSubstitution is the WILD SUBSTITUTION (Dean, 2026-08-08), kept through the flat island and through v31, and still the only change in this project that moved the number it was aimed at. When you pay the island, any single card it asks for may instead be paid with this many cards of any crops. null switches the rule off and restores exact matching, which is the control arm. It answers ticket 38's finding that the barn queue is a MATCHING problem and not a quantity one: 88.8% of barn-holding decisions could not afford any open tile and 84% of those were 1-2 cards short. Because a crate is 2 cards of ONE named suit, all or nothing, a single odd card of a suit is worth exactly zero and a barn fills with cards that can never combine - a parity trap. A rate of 2 breaks the trap at a real price. The property that makes 2 the right number rather than a tuned one: THE VALVE OPENS AS THE PRESSURE RISES. A 4-card barn can afford one substitution, a 12-card barn six, so the rule cannot cheapen delivery in the early game when barns are small and always rescues a jammed late game. Measured at n=500 it took the barn-glut assertion from 2.00 to 0.75, the median end-game barn from 4.5 to 1.5, removed the unfinished games and supply locks, and narrowed last-to-winner by 3.1 points. SCOPE IS LOAD-BEARING: island delivery ONLY. It must never reach the balloon move cost, a build cost, or anything else that spends barn cards, or the barn stops being a dead end and starts accelerating engines.

The END TRIGGER lives in rules.json (endGame.trigger = deliveryCount, deliveriesToTrigger = 6) rather than here, because it is no longer a property of any tile. It is FLAT at every seat count: 6 deliveries is half the 2-seat island's 12 delivery spaces, a third of the 3-seat island's 18 and a quarter of the 4-seat island's 24, so relative to the board the 2-player game runs longest. v31 makes turns materially more powerful, so this is the first knob to sweep after the pass lands.

Delivery cost is PER CRATE. A tile prints one crate icon per demand, a quantity label beside it, and one suit token slot per crate. The quantity label is the RATE, not the total - it reads 2=, meaning 2 cards of ONE suit per crate. A suit demand token is placed face up on every crate at setup, and paying a crate costs cardsPerCrate barn cards of that crate's suit. A cornucopia token is wild and accepts any suit at the same rate. Two crates on one tile may be dealt the same suit, in which case the tile wants 4 cards of one crop; that is the pool doing its job, not a bug.
seats counts players at the table. There is no one-seat board: a solo game is a two-seat game in which a bot occupies the second seat.

Exactly (seats + 1) suit decks are in play: one owned by each seat, plus one passive suit nobody farms but everybody may draw from and the island demands. The remaining suits are out of the game entirely. This is why the demand-token pool spans (seats + 1) suits - it spans exactly the decks on the table. NOTE THE DELIBERATE ASYMMETRY WITH THE MEEPLE BAG, which spans all five colours at every seat count: a demand token names a deck you must be able to draw from, a meeple names an action that exists whether or not its suit is on the table.

slotsBySeats is the authoritative layout table and is unchanged by the flat island and by v31 - the island is the same SIZE, it just has no hierarchy. It follows seats+1 / seats / seats-1 by level, giving 6 / 9 / 12 tiles and therefore 12 / 18 / 24 delivery spaces.

demandTokensBySeats grew with the crate count: every tile carries 2 crates, so the pool is tiles x 2 = 12 / 18 / 24, up from 10 / 16 / 22. Dean took a flat 4 tokens per suit at every seat count (one number to remember at the table) with the remainder in cornucopias, which puts the wild share at 0% / 11% / 17%. The 4-seat 17% is the highest the game has run and is the number to watch if the colour puzzle goes soft.

The pyramid layout is cosmetic in the strong sense: no tile is adjacent to any other, adjacency is null by decision rather than by omission, and since the level gate was deleted nothing constrains WHICH tile you deliver to. Any tile with a free delivery space is legal on any turn.

Bookend rule: the art paints each row's first printed face (A1 / B1 / C1) as the island's left edge and its last (A5 / B4 / C3) as the right edge, so a row with n tiles in play uses the first (n - 1) printed faces plus the row-end face. The 3-tile level-1 row is therefore A1, A2, A5.
At 2 seats the lone level-3 tile is D1 rather than C1. D1 prints no mechanical difference from C1; it is a distinct illustration for the two-player board.
unresolved: THE MEEPLE POOL COMPOSITION IS UNTESTED IN EVERY SENSE - never played, never simulated, and never argued for against an alternative. 5 per colour was chosen because 25 is the smallest flat bag that covers the 24 delivery spaces of a 4-seat board, which is a component argument and not a design one. The consequence named in the notes above is that the 4-seat island is nearly deterministic and the 2-seat island is not. overlays/meeple-pool-deep-v1.overlay.json is the paired arm.

Whether the island should offer the colours of the suits IN PLAY rather than all five. Ruled all five for v31 (a meeple's action exists regardless of who farms its suit) but the case against is real: at 2 seats, two of the five colours belong to nobody's Notice Board, so a Harvest meeple in a game with no Wheat seat is a free action nobody at the table can otherwise buy. That may be a feature. It has never been looked at.

D1 and C1 print identical cost and delivery capacity, and now that every tile is identical the two-seat substitution is purely illustrative. Confirm that is what is wanted, or drop D1 and let 2p use C3.

The flat 6-delivery end trigger is not scaled by seat count, and v31's more powerful turn makes that matter more, not less. If the 2-player game runs long at the table, the dial is either the trigger (a per-seat row) or slotsBySeats, not the VP.
